# Lavinia

*Mistress of the Gilded Stage*

## Personality

Grand, theatrical and ruthless about box-office takings. She treats every conversation as a performance.

## Lore

Lavinia is seventy-two, Mistress of the Gilded Stage, and she has never in her life simply entered a room. She arrives in it. She pauses in the doorway, lets the room notice her, and then crosses it as if there were an audience in the gallery, which, on Theatre Row, there very often is. She is grand, theatrical and utterly ruthless about box-office takings, and she treats every conversation as a performance, including the ones with her accountant, which are among her best.

### The oldest house on the Row

The Gilded Stage is the oldest theatre on Theatre Row, a tall, gilt-and-crimson house with a cheap gallery under the roof and a box kept for the palace that no one from the palace has sat in for many years. Lavinia walked through its stage door at fifteen, fifty-seven years ago, and asked for anything at all. She swept the stage for a season. Then an actress fell ill, and Lavinia, who had learned every line in the play from the wings, went on in her place and never came off again. For the next thirty-five years and more she played every great part in the house: queens and shepherdesses, murderesses and saints, the heroines of the war plays and the villains of the comedies.

The old manager who owned the house had no heirs, and thirty-five years ago, when he died, he left it to her. She has run it ever since. She played her last great part eighteen years ago and has played only the parts she chooses since, a wicked aunt here, a ghost there, so that audiences never quite forget whose house they are in. She never married. She says she has been married to the Gilded Stage for fifty-seven years and that it has been more faithful than any man and much more expensive.

### Her company

She has an eye for talent and no mercy in using it. Twenty-three years ago a girl from the old quarters called Rosamund came in and asked for a part, and Lavinia, still playing the great parts herself, gave her a line and a half as a maid with a letter. Rosamund made the audience applaud the letter. Lavinia has never quite forgiven her and has given her the best parts in the house ever since. Ten years ago she cast Rosamund opposite Percival, the Row's favourite hero, for the first time, and the two of them quarrelled so thoroughly on stage and off it that Lavinia has cast them together ever since, because the audiences love it and the box office loves it more.

Crispin has been her house playwright for fifteen years, and his comedies have paid for the roof twice. Tibb works her ropes and trapdoors and keeps the actors from killing each other, which Lavinia considers the most important job in the building after her own. Edith the costumer, who dressed her in the great parts, still argues with her about budgets every week, and they have both enjoyed it for decades.

### The bet

Lavinia wants one last triumph before she hands the Gilded Stage on. She has bet everything on it: the theatre's savings, a loan against the building, and her own name. The play is Crispin's Balrog War, the whole of it, from the First Burning to the weaving of the seal, the largest thing the Row has ever attempted. Crispin has written four acts and cannot find a fifth. Rosamund wants to play the Magician and will not share the stage with Percival. Percival wants the Savage warrior who held the Balrog at the Tree. Lavinia reminds Crispin roughly once a day that she has bet everything on him, in case he forgets. He has not forgotten.

She has not said to whom she will hand the theatre. People on the Row speculate about it constantly, which she enjoys.

### What she wants and fears

Lavinia wants a full house on opening night, a standing audience at the final curtain and the palace box occupied, just once, by the queen. What she fears is an empty gallery: audiences have begun going home earlier, and she can count the seats as well as anyone.

A quest might begin with Lavinia needing a rare prop or a real relic of the Balrog War for the stage, no questions asked, or with an anonymous letter promising that the play will never open.
